title: The Educated Barbarian: An introduction to Stoicism (Enchiridion analysis part 1)
summary: First episode on Epictetus' Enchiridion: what is in our power (opinion, movement, desire, aversion), resisting temptation and instant gratification, and good versus bad desire. He applies it to discipline, purposeful use of time, visualization and the fear of death.
claims: Marcus Aurelius is better for applying Stoicism day to day because the Meditations read like a personal log; Epictetus reads like orders but conveys meaning more clearly and cuts to the chase
Wanting others to share your opinions and getting upset when they don't wastes time and weakens your persuasion, because you are arguing for your own benefit rather than theirs
You do not choose your genetics, but you decide what you do with your body and therefore with those genetics
In a society that chases pleasure at any cost, simply controlling your desires already makes you more enlightened than most people
Negative feelings toward things or people are within your control; people blame others for them to escape responsibility for how they feel
No temptation is irresistible; treating desires like binge eating as spells you cannot resist is really choosing not to resist, and recognizing free will gives you that power
Instant gratification is the greatest trap: taking the pleasure before doing the work means the work never gets done, and any dopamine you get without paying is billed later
Desire is not bad in itself; it is what sets you in motion, e.g. wanting a muscular physique is what gets you training. Stoicism does not reject desire or mortify the soul
He distrusts doctrines that claim bodily privations such as nofap lead to enlightenment; be strict with the mind first and the body follows by default

Desire has three outcomes: getting something that is bad for you, falling into what you wanted to avoid, or getting something good for you and the community; feed the last kind, which takes the most time and energy so most people avoid it
Do not worry about the unavoidable parts of sickness and death; prepare your body to stay healthy and live long, but do not overstress about what you cannot control
Becoming overweight and unhealthy is contrary to nature and is within your power to refuse
If something is truly worth pursuing, its payback will not come tomorrow; delayed gratification marks worthwhile goals
Constantly ask why you are drawn to something: the caveman brain chases sex, food and instant pleasure that no longer serve survival, and questioning it builds a strong anti-hedonistic mind
Everyone is a dopamine junkie; being a slave to dopamine is the quickest way to ruin your life
Everything he does has a goal, sometimes two years away; when he deliberately disconnects he allows himself about 20 minutes before getting back to work
Killing time is escapism; if you do not think about what you are doing you will look back and realize you did nothing
Pre-visualize scenarios such as a home intruder (hiding spots, weapons, escape routes, who to protect); once thought through it is settled, so it does not make you paranoid
Men are disturbed by their opinions about things rather than the things themselves; the fear of death comes from mankind's collective opinion, not experience
Someone who accepts death dies peacefully, while someone terrified of it creates their own hell
Like the samurai, think about your death every day, without romanticizing it through religion; it is part of life and brings wisdom
